name: Royal Blue (Dark)
lede: Royal Blue (Dark) is a near-black navy blue built by darkening [[royal-blue|Royal Blue]], not a color coined under its own name.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new word
sections.body:
Royal Blue (Dark) takes the word "dark" and attaches it to Royal Blue rather than being coined on its own [1]. The parent name is the one with a history: it is carried by CSS and X11, the 2010 xkcd crowd survey, the 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary and the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary, which first records it in 1892 at plate 43, swatch D 12 [1]. Wikipedia's entry for Royal Blue separately credits Crayola, and the 1955 ISCC-NBS system filed the plain name at block 179 [1].

Nothing in our library explains who darkened Royal Blue into this exact swatch, or when, so the modifier itself is undocumented [1]. The nearest color by our look-alike data is [[navy|Navy]], 4.5 units away and read as a duller version of this blue, with [[st-patrick-s-blue|St. Patrick's Blue]] a little further off at 4.7, read as more vivid and lighter [2].

sections.title: How dark is dark
sections.body: On screen this measures lightness 16 out of 100, far below the mid-tone Royal Blue it modifies [1]. [[midnight-blue|Midnight Blue]] sits in the same dark-blue cluster, 5.5 units off and read as more vivid and more purple [2]. Treat the hex as a screen approximation only: no pigment, dye or paint-chip sample backs this specific value [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this exact dark blue in 2 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed [3]. The earlier is a mid-19th-century Spanish royal portrait, *Berenguela reina de León y Castilla* by Francisco Prats y Velasco (1850), where it covers about 6 percent of the canvas [3]. The other is Maurice Denis's *Portrait of Yvonne Lerolle in three views* (1897), where it covers about 11 percent [3]. Spain and France are the only countries it turns up in at this threshold, both on samples too thin to generalize from [3]. The count is a computed color match on varnished, photographed paintings, not a pigment identification [3].
